title: Al-Quddus, the Most Pure
hookLine: the Most Pure, beyond every flaw, and a bucket of water poured in the mosque instead of shouting
tomorrow: why greet a total stranger with a name of God?

cards: A full glass tips across a nice dinner table, and every head turns to whoever knocked it. Now the mosque in Medina. A Bedouin, a man from the desert, walks in, goes to a corner, and relieves himself right there.
People leap up, shouting at him. And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says: leave him alone. What would you do next?

teach.b: He asked for a bucket of water to be poured over the spot.
Bukhari records what he told the angry crowd, in paraphrase: you were sent to make things easy, not to make them hard.

In Muslim's version, he then called the man over and explained, gently, that mosques aren't for this; they're for remembering Allah, for prayer and the Qur'an. The place got clean, and the man kept his dignity.

That answers yesterday's question from the ground up. Al-Quddus, from the root q-d-s, is the Most Pure: beyond every flaw, free of anything unworthy. Pickthall's list in Surah al-Hashr calls Him the Holy One.
Nothing in creation is pure like that.
People spill, stain, and get things wrong; Al-Quddus never needs cleaning.
So for people, purity is something done, again and again, with water and care, like that bucket.
Not disgust at a mess. The clean-up, done without shaming anyone. Something to tell a friend tonight: when the mosque itself was soiled, the Prophet's first instruction was to stop the shouting.

how: Muslims keep the places and clothes of prayer clean, and wash with water before prayer; in the bowing and prostration some say subbuhun quddus, glorified, holy.

o: the Most Hidden, beyond all sight
the Most Pure, beyond every flaw
the Most Strict about every rule

games.q: the bucket of water — tap the pairs.

s: the Prophet had the Bedouin thrown out of the mosque
he said leave him alone, had water poured over the spot, then explained gently.
the story ends with: you were sent to make things easy, not hard
being pure means never getting dirty
only Al-Quddus is beyond every flaw; for people, purity is the cleaning, done again and again.

games.q: at a family dinner, your little cousin knocks a full plate onto your aunt's new rug. two uncles start yelling at him. what would the bucket-of-water story do first?
o: stop the yelling, clean it up together, and explain gently later.
let them yell; he has to learn some things have to be respected.
clean it yourself in silence so nobody has to talk about it.
games.why: leave him alone, pour the water, then teach gently: the place got clean and the man kept his dignity.

practice: Pick one small thing within reach: your phone screen, your glasses, a mug. Clean it slowly, as if it belonged to someone you respect. For the sit, set it down and look at it, clear.

wordCard.voice: Al-Quddus: the Most Pure, the Holy One, beyond every flaw. People are cleaned again and again; He never needs it.

orig.note: Arabic: the Most Pure, the Holy One, from q-d-s, holiness.

carryVoice: One word to carry: pure, the kind of clean that leaves everyone their dignity. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 220 (the Bedouin in the mosque: leave him, pour a bucket of water; you were sent to make things easy, not difficult)
Sahih Muslim 285 (he then called the man and explained that mosques are for remembering Allah, prayer and the Qur'an)
